topic: Algorithmic hiring tools are recreating historical biases under the guise of objectivity
subject: technology

sources.title: Discriminated by an algorithm: a systematic review of discrimination and fairness by algorithmic decision-making in the context of HR recruitment and HR development
Algorithmic Bias in AI-Based Recruitment Systems: Implications for Fair Hiring Practices
Artificial intelligence bias in medical system designs: a systematic review
Mitigating Cognitive Biases in Developing AI-Assisted Recruitment Systems
Bias and Fairness in LLM-Based Recruitment: A Systematic Review

facts.claim: Technical studies rarely engage with HCAI design principles, while governance-oriented work rarely operationalizes the technical limitations documented in empirical literature.
facts.quote: Technical studies rarely engage with HCAI design principles governance-oriented work rarely operationalizes the technical limitations that the empirical literature has documented in detail.

facts.claim: Incomplete specifications in design protocols and weak AI design exploited for prediction are linked to data bias and algorithmic bias in healthcare studies.
facts.quote: the majority of the studies in healthcare suffer from data bias and algorithmic bias due to incomplete specifications mentioned in the design protocol and weak AI design exploited for prediction.

facts.claim: AI-recruitment systems may fail to achieve unbiased decisions about applicants because they can replicate and amplify human biases.
facts.quote: There are risks of encoding biases in the datasets and algorithms of AI which lead AIRS to replicate and amplify human biases.

facts.claim: Knowledge sharing between HR managers and AI developers is linked to mitigating biases in AI-recruitment systems by informing data labeling and understanding job functions.
facts.quote: The findings show that knowledge sharing can help to mitigate biases in AIRS by informing data labeling, understanding job functions, and improving the machine learning model.

facts.claim: AI-driven recruitment systems are linked to significant concerns regarding algorithmic bias, fairness, transparency, and accountability.
facts.quote: While AI-driven recruitment systems improve efficiency and decision-making, they also introduce significant concerns regarding algorithmic bias, fairness, transparency, and accountability.

research.angle: While AI-recruitment systems are linked to replicating human biases and data-driven inaccuracies, there is a structural disconnect between the technical documentation of these limitations and the governance frameworks intended to manage them.
research.verdict: The evidence confirms that AI-recruitment systems can replicate human biases and suffer from design-related flaws, but it highlights a gap between identifying these risks and operationalizing technical solutions.
research.caveat: The sources focus heavily on identifying risks and theoretical frameworks rather than providing specific data on the exact proxies used for protected classes.
